note: Part B (drawing) is not transcribed: no model answer exists.

questions.text: Count the number of circles in the given figure.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Ignore the wavy closed red line, which is not a circle, and count the circles colour by colour. There are 8 teal circles, 9 red circles, 4 dark blue circles and 1 small yellow circle. In total that is 8 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 22 circles.

questions.text: Shown here are different types of leaves. Count how many types of leaves there are.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Group the leaves by their outline, not by size or how they are turned. The types are: smooth and rounded, smooth and pointed (teardrop), angular with straight wavy sides, lobed with hooked points, lobed with rounded cloud-like lobes, broad with finely toothed edges, broad with coarsely toothed edges, and narrow with toothed edges. That makes 8 types.

questions.text: Count the number of squares in the given figure.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Both octagons are drawn the same way, so count one and then add any square that uses both. Inside one octagon there are 4 small corner squares, 1 central square, 4 large squares along the sides, 4 small tilted diamonds, 1 tilted square in the centre and 4 large tilted squares that use an octagon side: 18 squares. The two octagons give 36, and where they meet the diagonal lines form one more tilted square, so the total is 37.

questions.text: Shown here are letters of an alphabet, from A to Z. How many of these letters, if flipped along the horizontal axis, can still be read as capital letters?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Flip each letter about a horizontal line through its middle and ask whether the result still reads as a capital letter, either the same one or another. Letters whose top and bottom halves mirror each other stay the same, and some letters in this typeface turn into others (a triangle A becomes the V shape, M becomes W). IIT Bombay's final key gives 14 letters.

questions.text: Count the number of fonts used in the given set of words.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Group the words by the shapes of their letters, not by size or weight: compare serifs, the contrast between thick and thin strokes, the ends of strokes and letters such as a, g and e. A word in the same design at a different size or weight belongs to the same font. IIT Bombay's final key gives 9 fonts.

questions.text:
The five most recent cricket scores of four teams are as follows:

| Team 1 | Team 2 | Team 3 | Team 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 255 | 301 | 309 | 288 |
| 278 | 282 | 319 | 301 |
| 291 | 269 | 279 | 322 |
| 268 | 299 | 312 | 310 |
| 308 | 279 | 316 | 289 |

Based on this information, identify the team with the most consistent performance (least variance in scores), and write its average.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The averages are 280, 286, 307 and 302. The sums of squared deviations from the mean are 1678 for Team 1, 748 for Team 2, 1038 for Team 3 and 830 for Team 4. Team 2 varies least, so the answer is its average, 1430 divided by 5, which is 286.

questions.text: Count the number of spelling mistakes in the given passage.
questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The misspelt words are thier (their), conseintious (conscientious), recieve (receive), atitudes (attitudes), beginings (beginnings), bee (been) and comonplace (commonplace). Words such as doctrinaires and paterfamilias are spelt correctly. That gives 7 mistakes.

questions.text: Shown below are three types of interlocking rods. There are total 12 rods, of which 6 are type A, 2 are type B and 4 are type C respectively. What is the maximum length that can be achieved by connecting the rods appropriately?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Type A has a 1 cm peg at both ends, type B has a socket at one end and a peg at the other, and type C has sockets at both ends. A joint always pairs a peg with a socket, so A and C rods must alternate in a chain, with B rods slotted in anywhere. With only 4 C rods, at most 5 A rods fit: A C A C A C A C A, plus both B rods. The rod bodies add up to 5 x 8 + 4 x 4 + 2 x 6 = 68 cm, and the two pegs left sticking out at the ends add 2 cm, giving 70 cm.

questions.text: The given figure is made of letters L, T, H, I, E and F, set in different orientations. Find the total number of occurrences of capital letter T in the figure.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Each letter is a separate group of touching strokes. A T is the only letter made of exactly two strokes where the end of one meets the middle of the other: an L joins two strokes at their ends, and E, F and H use three or four strokes. Checking every group in the figure this way, and confirming each by eye, gives 7 Ts.

questions.text: Shown below, to the left, are three types of pencils: A, B and C. Find the total number of type A pencils in the figure on the right, which shows various pencils pointing in either of the two directions, up or down.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Type A pointing up reads black, white, white from left to right; turned to point down it reads white, white, black. Type B reads white, black, white and type C black, white, black either way. Splitting the right-hand figure into its 16 pencils using the tips, 4 up-pointing pencils read black, white, white and 3 down-pointing pencils read white, white, black, so 7 pencils are type A.

questions.text: Count the total number of parallelograms in the given figure.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Every line runs in one of the two directions of the big rhombus, so a parallelogram is chosen by two lines of each direction whose drawn segments cover all four sides. Checking each such choice gives 15, including the whole figure and the smallest pieces.

questions.text: Imagine letters are extruded into three dimensional objects, as shown in the figure on the left (the letter A). If the word LOVE (shown on the right) were to be extruded, how many surfaces would it have?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: An extruded letter has a front face, a back face and one side surface for every straight edge or continuous curve of its outline. L has 6 edges, so 8 surfaces. O has one outer and one inner curved surface, so 4. V (flat bottom) has 7 edges, so 9. E has 12 edges, so 14. Together 8 + 4 + 9 + 14 = 35.

questions.text: Count the number of unique patterns in the given grid.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Compare the 49 cells by texture and tone. They fall into 7 clearly different patterns, each repeated several times: two light dotted textures, two mid-grey textures, a smooth grey hatch and two dark textures. So there are 7 unique patterns.

questions.text:
In photography, f-numbers represent lens aperture. Write the missing f-number in the sequence below.

f/2.8, f/3.2, f/3.5, f/__, f/4.5, f/5.0, f/5.6
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The sequence is the standard one-third-stop scale. Between f/2.8 and f/5.6 (two full stops) the marked values are 2.8, 3.2, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5.0 and 5.6, and f/4 is itself a full stop. So the missing number is 4.

questions.text: Given below are eight pieces of a puzzle. Arranged correctly they form a four digit number. What is the number formed after the correct arrangement?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Turn each piece until its pink strokes read upright, then fit the cut edges together so the dark background forms one rectangle. The strokes then join into four digits: 2, 8, 2 and 3, giving the number 2823.

questions.text:
The following excerpt is from an article on Indonesian Shadow Puppet Theatre:

"Muslim Indonesia is a fascinating story of tolerance and absorption, a relaxed compromise between religions, unlike any of the other multi-faith societies. Wayang Kulit---'skin theatre'---is an ancient Indonesian art of shadow theatre. Historically, performances in the Theatre of Shadows featured Hindu epics and lasted throughout the night. Light from an oil lamp behind the puppeteer's head cast the shadows from the puppets onto a white sheet. Some members of the audience---usually the women and children---sit on the shadow side of the screen, while the men would sit on the favoured other side, where the features and colours of the puppets could be seen. The puppeteer, known as a dalang, would not only control the puppets, but also conduct the accompanying music, performed by a gamelan orchestra".

The following statements have been derived based on both explicit and implicit reading of the above passage:

I. Indonesian society accorded pre-eminence to women and children.
II. Modern Wayang Kulit probably uses electric lights to cast shadows.
III. Wayang Kulit had Islamic origins.
IV. Gamelan is a traditional ensemble music of Java and Bali in Indonesia.
V. The puppets are made of fabric for easy manipulation by the dalang.

How many of the above statements are FALSE?
questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: Statement I is false: the men sat on the favoured side, so women and children were not given pre-eminence. II is a fair implicit reading, since the oil lamp is described as historical. III is false: the shows featured Hindu epics. IV is true: the gamelan is the traditional ensemble of Java and Bali. V is false: Wayang Kulit means skin theatre, so the puppets are leather. That makes 3 false statements.

questions.text: Shown below is a belt and pulley arrangement. How many pulleys are rotating clockwise?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Follow the belt from A, which turns anticlockwise as the belt rises on its right side. The belt runs over the top of B moving left (anticlockwise), up the left of C (clockwise), round the right and top of D (anticlockwise), under E moving right (anticlockwise), over F moving right (clockwise), round the bottom of G (clockwise), over H moving right (clockwise) and down the right of I (clockwise). So C, F, G, H and I turn clockwise: 5 pulleys.

questions.text: Two views of the same solid object are shown below. Count the number of surfaces the solid object has.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Use both views together to build up the solid, then count its surfaces one region at a time: the top and bottom, each outer wall, and every face of each step, slope and groove, counting a curved face as one surface. Tick each one off on the views so that no face is counted twice. IIT Bombay's final key gives 18 surfaces.

questions.text: Count the number of cubes in the given figure. No cube has been removed from parts of the figure that are not visible.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The figure is a 6 by 6 by 6 block (216 cubes) with cubes taken out of the visible top and front, and nothing is missing from hidden parts. Count column by column, from the back-left row to the front row, as heights read off the figure: 6, 6, 5, 6, 6, 6 (35); 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6 (31); 3, 5, 4, 4, 5, 5 (26, where the front column has a gap under a floating cube and holds 3); 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6 (24); 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (21); and 2, 3, 2, 3, 5, 6 (21, where one column has a gap under its top cube and holds 5). The total is 35 + 31 + 26 + 24 + 21 + 21 = 158.

questions.text:
A, B, C, D, E and F are six robots. Each robot can contact some other robots, though none of the robots can contact all the robots. The rules of contacting are as follows:

B can contact E and can be contacted by C
D can be contacted by A, E and F
F can contact C
D can contact C and E
F can be contacted by A

A robot can receive a message from other robots that can contact it and can relay the message to another robot it is allowed to contact. What is the minimum number of robots that are required between robot A and robot B, to send a message from robot A to robot B?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: A can contact only D and F. Neither D nor F can contact B directly, so at least two robots are needed in between. The only robot that can contact B is C, and both D and F can contact C, so A to F to C to B (or A to D to C to B) works. The minimum is 2.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Jacques Lacan was a French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist.

options.label: B
options.text: Claude Lévi-Strauss is called the father of structural anthropology.

options.label: C
options.text: Michel Foucault was a French writer who wrote, "Being and Nothingness".

options.label: D
options.text: Ferdinand de Saussure was a Swiss linguist and semiotician.

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Jacques Lacan was a French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist, and Claude Levi-Strauss is called the father of structural anthropology. Ferdinand de Saussure was a Swiss linguist and a founder of semiotics. C is false: Being and Nothingness was written by Jean-Paul Sartre, not Michel Foucault.

questions.text: Which of the four figures shown on the right exactly fit the figure shown on the left?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.subtopic: Matching a part to the whole
questions.solution: Each piece has one straight edge and a toothed edge, and fills the hollow on one side of the goblet shape up to a straight line. Pieces I and III have teeth spaced to match the right-hand hollow, and pieces II and IV match the left-hand hollow (the goblet is symmetric, so its two hollows are mirror images). Every piece fits, so the pairs I and II, II and III, and I and IV all fit, and option D is wrong.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Ellora caves contain Hindu Shaivaite sculptures.

options.label: B
options.text: Elephanta caves contain only Hindu Vaishnavaite sculptures.

options.label: C
options.text: Ellora caves contain only Hindu Shaivaite sculptures.

options.label: D
options.text: Elephanta caves contain Hindu Shaivaite sculptures.

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Ellora has Hindu, Buddhist and Jain caves, and its Hindu caves, such as the Kailasa temple, are rich in Shaivaite sculpture, so A is true and C (only Shaivaite) is false. Elephanta is famous for Shaivaite sculpture such as the Trimurti and Shiva as Nataraja, so D is true and B is false.

questions.text: Which of the given figures can be drawn without either lifting the pen or retracing any line?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A connected figure can be drawn in one stroke without retracing a line when no point has an odd number of lines meeting at it. In all four figures every point has an even number of lines (2, 4 or 6), so all four can be drawn this way. B (I, II and III), C (IV) and D (all of the figures) each name only figures that can be drawn, so all three are correct; A (none of the figures) is wrong.

questions.text: The triangular shape (at left) is broken into several parts. Choose the correct set of parts from the figures (on the right) to put the triangle together again.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The curved hollow in A is a quarter circle, and the quarter-circle part of C fills it exactly once C is given a quarter turn. Together they make a trapezoid whose base equals the triangle base and whose slanted sides match the triangle sides. The small triangle D, a smaller copy of the whole triangle, sits on top. B is the wrong size and is not needed.

questions.text: The given heart shape (on top) is made of different parts put together. Which of the shapes in the options can be constructed using all the parts of the given heart shape?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Take the heart side as 2 units. Its pieces are a 2 by 2 square cut into a small square, a small triangle, a parallelogram and a trapezium (these four rebuild the 2 by 2 square), one semicircle of radius 1 and two quarter circles of radius 1. So every answer must use straight-edged area 4 and curved parts that make one full circle of radius 1. B is a 2 by 2 square with the semicircle on top and the two quarter circles joined into a semicircle below. C is the semicircle on a 2 by 2 square with a quarter circle at each bottom corner, forming the brim. A and D have only 3 square units of straight-edged area (D is a circle on a 1 by 3 bar), so they cannot use all the parts.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Ustad Mansur was a painter during the reign of Jahangir, and he is well known for depicting plants and animals.

options.label: B
options.text: The painting of "Emperor Jahangir Weighs Prince Khurram" in the Tuzk-e-Jahangiri is attributed to Manohar Das.

options.label: C
options.text: Govardhan was a painter during the reigns of Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan. He was one of the illustrators of the Baburnama.

options.label: D
options.text: Nainsukh was a court painter during the reign of Aurangzeb, and he is well known for painting several of Aurangzeb’s portraits.

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Ustad Mansur was Jahangir's court painter, famous for his studies of birds, animals and flowers. The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri painting of Jahangir weighing Prince Khurram is attributed to Manohar (Manohar Das). Govardhan worked under Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan and contributed illustrations to the Baburnama. Nainsukh was a Pahari painter of Guler who worked for Raja Balwant Singh of Jasrota, not a court painter of Aurangzeb, so D is false.

questions.text: A square with four sets of symbols in it (shown below, at left) is to be divided into four equal parts such that each part has all four symbols in it. Which of the four shapes shown below (at right) fulfill(s) the condition?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Read the grid row by row: diamond, heart, club, spade; club, spade, heart, diamond; heart, diamond, spade, club; spade, heart, diamond, club. Every row holds all four suits, so four 1 by 4 strips (A) work. For the T shape (B), the 4 by 4 square splits into four T pieces in one way and each of them holds all four suits. No split of the square into four L pieces (C) or four S pieces (D) gives every piece all four suits; the S shape cannot fill the square at all.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The Lion Capital of Ashoka found in Sarnath is carved out of granite rock.

options.label: B
options.text: The Ellora caves are carved in granite rock.

options.label: C
options.text: The descent of the Ganges in Mahabalipuram is carved out of granite rock.

options.label: D
options.text: The Ajanta caves are carved in basalt rock.

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The Descent of the Ganges (Arjuna's Penance) at Mahabalipuram is carved on granite boulders, and the Ajanta caves are cut into basalt rock of the Deccan Traps. The Lion Capital at Sarnath is polished Chunar sandstone, not granite, and the Ellora caves are carved in basalt, not granite.

questions.text: Which of the options is/are simple rotations of the given figure?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Compare each grid with the given 6 by 6 grid cell by cell. D matches the given grid turned through 180 degrees. A and C are its mirror image (left and right swapped), which no rotation can produce, and B matches neither a rotation nor the mirror image.

questions.text: Which of these paintings is/are by Paul Klee?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: A is Paul Klee's Park bei Lu (Park near Lucerne), with his thick black brush strokes on soft colour fields. B is Klee's Comedy, ghostly figures on a dark ground. D, with fragmented bright colour patches and black linear signs, is also a late Klee. C is Pablo Picasso's The Kitchen (1948), a grey line drawing of circles and nodes.

questions.text: Which of the following terms relate(s) to printmaking?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Serigraphy is screen printing, lithography prints from a flat stone or plate using the repulsion of oil and water, and etching uses acid to bite lines into a metal plate: all three are printmaking methods. Cartography is the making of maps, not a printmaking technique.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Kuntaka was a Kashmiri Sanskrit poetician and literary theorist who is known for his work Vakroktijivitam in which he postulates the Vakrokti Siddhanta.

options.label: B
options.text: Abhinavagupta was a Kashmiri aesthetician well known for his commentary on the Natya Shastra and for introducing the Shanta Rasa.

options.label: C
options.text: Mammata Bhatta was the author of Dhvanyaloka, and is credited with creating "Dhvani Theory".

options.label: D
options.text: Anandavardhana was a Sanskrit rhetorician from Kashmir, and is credited with writing the Kavya Prakasa a work on poetry and rhetoric.

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Kuntaka, a Kashmiri theorist, wrote the Vakroktijivita and set out the theory of vakrokti. Abhinavagupta wrote the Abhinavabharati commentary on the Natya Shastra and established Shanta (peace) as a rasa. The Dhvanyaloka and the dhvani theory are by Anandavardhana, not Mammata, and the Kavya Prakasha is by Mammata, not Anandavardhana, so C and D swap the two authors.

questions.text: Shown below are three objects in 3D --- one cube and two right-angled prisms. Assume that they can be merged into each other to form one 3D object. From the options given below, choose the possible object(s) that can be formed by this merging.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Each prism has a right-angled triangle face with hypotenuse 2 and height 1 (legs about 1.41), and is 1 deep. A is the cube with the two prisms placed end to end as a roof. B has one prism on the back half of the top and the other against the back half of the right face, their sloping faces in one plane. C has the two prisms crossing each other on top, which is possible because they may merge. D has the two prisms side by side against the front face, legs on the ground and on the face, giving a slope that rises 1.41 and leaves a 0.59 vertical band below the top.

questions.text: Shown below are steps in creating a pattern. From the options given below, identify the element(s) that can be repeated in order to create this pattern.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The tile's outline is symmetric left to right and top to bottom, so one quarter of it, reflected, gives the whole tile, and the pattern is made of these tiles sharing edges. B is exactly the top-left quarter and D is the same quarter flipped top to bottom, so either can be repeated to make the pattern. A fits only if copies are allowed to overlap at a shared point, and C does not match the outline.

questions.text: Which of these paintings is/are by Anjali Ila Menon?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Anjolie Ela Menon paints elongated figures with large dark eyes in translucent, layered colour, often with animals such as goats and crows. A, B and D show this style. C is Amrita Sher-Gil's The Bride's Toilet: women around a seated bride, painted in flat earthy colours.

questions.text:
A person has six daughters, P, Q, R, S, T and U, who live in four metros. They are a Pilot, Accountant, Diplomat, Banker, Commando, and Teacher.

Three daughters are married.
S, who lives in Mumbai, is a Diplomat.
Those staying in Kolkata are the Commando and the Accountant.
One of the two Mumbaiites is married, while two of the unmarried ones live in Kolkata and Delhi respectively.
The Teacher lives in Chennai.
T, the Accountant, is married.
U lives in Mumbai and P, in Delhi.
Q is a Commando, and Commandos do not marry.

Which of the following assertions is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: If the Banker is unmarried, then the pilot is P.

options.label: B
options.text: R is the teacher, and lives in Chennai.

options.label: D
options.text: If the Diplomat is married, then so is the Banker.

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Q is the Commando, so Q lives in Kolkata and is unmarried; T, the married Accountant, also lives in Kolkata. S and U live in Mumbai and P in Delhi, so R is the one in Chennai and must be the Teacher (B true). The unmarried daughter in Delhi is P, so P and Q are unmarried; with T, one of S and U, and R married, there are three married. P and U share Pilot and Banker. A fails: the Banker could be the unmarried P with U as Pilot. D fails: if S is married then U is unmarried, and the Banker (P or U) is unmarried. C is true.

questions.text: Select the statement(s) about the Indus Valley Civilization that is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: At its peak, the Indus Valley Civilization encompassed nearly 200,000 Square Miles.

options.label: B
options.text: Stone seals from the Indus Valley Civilization have been found as far afield as Greece and Macedonia.

options.label: C
options.text: The largest of the Indus Valley cities, such as Harappa and Mohen-jo-Daro, had populations of a 100,000 people and more.

options.label: D
options.text: Despite the existence of highly ordered cities in the Indus Valley, there is no evidence of kings or pharaohs or any leader at all.

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The Indus Valley Civilization was the largest of the early civilizations, spread over a very large area (statement A), and its well planned cities show no palaces, royal tombs or images of kings, so there is no clear evidence of rulers (statement D). Indus seals have been found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf, not in Greece or Macedonia. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are estimated at about 30,000 to 60,000 people, well short of 100,000.

questions.text:
The Green Revolution has arguably been the most striking technological triumph of the 20th century in the realm of food production and land yields. Yet, there are serious concerns about its ill-effects on the environment.

Read the following paragraph and answer the question related to it. Which of the following concerns is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The disruption of the Nitrogen cycle by the massive use of chemical fertilizers is unsustainable for the environment.

options.label: B
options.text: The Green Revolution has unequivocally been the most striking technological triumph of the 20th century in the realm of food production.

options.label: C
options.text: Large monocultures of crops brought about by the Green Revolution are susceptible to sudden destruction by pests and disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing the supply of food through the Green Revolution would encourage the appearance of more and more new individuals, leading to worldwide famine as the human population becomes limitless.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: Heavy use of chemical fertilisers upsets the nitrogen cycle (runoff, polluted water, damaged soil), and vast single-crop fields can be wiped out by one pest or disease: both are real environmental concerns. B only repeats the praise in the passage and is not a concern. D is an exaggerated claim of limitless population and worldwide famine, not an environmental ill-effect.

questions.text:
There are many subtleties to designing with audio in order to create useful, non-intrusive experiences that offer instruction, information, and feedback when users interact with everyday devices, such as mobile phones, cars, toys etc.

Read the following paragraph and answer the question related to it. If audio might play a part in your design, what are some considerations, with specific regard to cognitive loads on users and aesthetics of interaction that you must keep in mind? Pick all that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: Audio is linear, time-sensitive, and transient, therefore good design must limit the number of audio menu options.

options.label: B
options.text: Users will often listen to all choices before picking one, and a long list limits their ability to remember them all. So it is necessary to keep choices pertinent and parsimonious.

options.label: C
options.text: Using jargon in instruction enhances user experience, since it enables users to create shortcuts more easily, and to utilize the offered functionality of a device in wider and deeper ways.

options.label: D
options.text: It is good to differentiate between a novice user and an expert user by keeping track of the number of interactions that the user has with the device, and tailoring an audio experience for first-time users, while playing shortened prompts to expert users.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: Audio plays once in order and then is gone, so menus must be short (A), and users who hear all options before choosing cannot hold a long list in memory, so choices should be few and relevant (B). Giving first-time users full prompts and regular users shortened ones fits the experience to the person (D). Jargon raises the mental effort of understanding instructions, so C is wrong.

questions.text:
Anaximander, in the sixth century BCE, had a theory of evolution, and maintained that men are descended from fishes. This was philosophy because it was a speculation unsupported by detailed evidence, but Darwin's theory of evolution was science, because it was based on the succession of forms of life as found in fossils, and upon the distribution of animals and plants in many parts of the world. A man might say, with enough truth to justify a joke: 'Science is what we know and philosophy is what we don't know.' But it should be added that philosophical speculation as to what we do not yet know has shown itself a valuable preliminary to exact scientific knowledge. The guesses of the Pythagoreans in astronomy, of Anaximander and Empedocles in biological evolution, and of Democritus as to the atomic constitution of matter, provided the men of science in later times with hypotheses which, but for the philosophers, might never have entered their heads. We may say that, on its theoretical side, philosophy consists, at least in part, in the framing of large general hypotheses which science is not yet in a position to test; but when it becomes possible to test the hypotheses they become, if verified, a part of science, and cease to count as ‘philosophy’.

Read the following paragraph and answer the question related to it. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE of the paragraph above?

options.label: A
options.text: Even though Anaximander had a theory of evolution in the sixth century BCE that seems untenable to our modern minds, the author explains how philosophical speculation is rigorous enough to have spawned scientific hypotheses that have often proved entirely plausible and empirically provable in later times.

options.label: B
options.text: Anaximander’s philosophical speculation on the theory of evolution, as far back as the sixth century BCE, is implausible given the evidence that supports Darwin’s theory of evolution, and the tone of the passage seems to suggest that the author finds such idle conjecture as being---at best---immaterial to the trajectories of actual science.

options.label: C
options.text: Even though Anaximander had a theory of evolution in the sixth century BCE that seems untenable to our modern minds, the author explains that philosophy is often the source of the large frameworks that inform and inspire scientific imagination.

options.label: D
options.text: Between the speculations of Pythagoreans in astronomy, Anaximander and Empedocles in biological evolution, and Democritus on the atomic constitution of matter, the author bemoans the loss of later advances in scientific understanding---though based on these conjectures---from being considered as also belonging to philosophy.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The author says philosophers' guesses, such as Anaximander's on evolution, gave later scientists hypotheses they might never have had, and that such hypotheses become science once they are tested and verified. A states this, and C says the same in other words: philosophy supplies the large frameworks that inspire scientific thinking. B is wrong because the author calls speculation a valuable preliminary to science, not immaterial to it. D is wrong because the author does not complain that verified ideas stop counting as philosophy; he simply says they do.

questions.text: Identify which of the options given below can be folded to make the 3D object in the picture shown below.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The object is a tall thin slab standing on the diameter of a short rounded base, with a half cylinder on each side. Every net has the base (a rounded oval with two short flat edges), the slab's two narrow end faces as long strips from the flat edges, the two curved half-cylinder walls, and one long rounded strip made of a half-cylinder top, the exposed upper part of one side of the slab, the slab top, the other exposed side and the other half-cylinder top. In A and C each curved wall is hinged at the base end of an end strip on its own side and the long strip folds over correctly (A along the side of an end strip, C at its top). In B the exposed side panels of the long strip are only as tall as the slab is thick, so the slab sides would not close. In D the long strip is hinged one panel too low on the end strip and one curved wall is missing, its place taken by a single over-long strip.

questions.text: Shown below are four structures made with rigid elements. They are joined to each other at red points by screws that allow elements to move. Identify the structure/s that is/are NOT rigid.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A pin-jointed frame is rigid only if it is built from triangles. A is a closed loop of six bars through six pins (the middle bar crosses the diagonal without a pin), so it can deform. In B the right-hand part is a triangle, but the left bar is held by a single pin and can swing freely. C is a five-bar loop with no triangle, so it can collapse. D is a triangle (the two crossing bars pinned at their crossing and joined by the bottom bar), so it is rigid.

questions.text: Which of the statements is/are TRUE with respect to the picture shown below?

options.label: A
options.text: A and B need to be strong in tension, and C and E in compression.

options.label: B
options.text: C needs to be strong in tension, and A and D in compression.

options.label: C
options.text: C and D need to be strong in tension.

options.label: D
options.text: B needs to be strong in compression, and all others need to be strong in tension.

questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The stool legs (B) carry the sitter's weight, so they are in compression, while the rung (A) between splayed legs stops them spreading and is pulled in tension. A fishing line (C), stretched umbrella fabric (D) and a sock pulled over a foot (E) are all in tension. So C (C and D in tension) and D (B in compression, the rest in tension) are both true; A and B wrongly put the rung, line, fabric or sock in compression.

questions.text: Which of the statements is/are TRUE about the FIVE symbols given below?

options.label: C
options.text: Only one is not a musical note.

options.label: D
options.text: At least three are musical notes.

questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Symbol A is a half note (minim) and E is an eighth note (quaver), so both are notes. B is the bass (F) clef and D is the treble (G) clef: clefs fix the pitch of the staff lines and are not notes. C is the flat sign, which lowers a note by a semitone. Counting the two clefs as the only non-notes makes B (two are not notes) and D (at least three are notes) true.

questions.text: Shown below are three panels with cutouts in three shapes. From the given pairs of blocks, identify which pairs will PASS THROUGH all the cutouts.

options.label: D
options.text: All pairs A, B and C

questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Every block is a thick plate, and a block may be turned before it is pushed through. Edge-on, each block shows only a narrow rectangle (its length by its thickness), which slides through the long horizontal slot of the third panel and the arms of the cross in the second. Face-on, the cloud block fits the cloud of the first panel, and the T, cross and L shapes all fit the cross and the tree outline or go through edge-on. Since no block is longer than the slots, all three pairs pass through every cutout.

questions.text: Which of the materials given below was/were used for writing on in ancient India?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Ancient Indian manuscripts were written on dried palm leaves (especially in the south and east) and on birch bark, called bhurjapatra, in the north and in Kashmir. Coconut leaves and bamboo leaves were not used as writing surfaces.

questions.text: Shown are logos of different Companies/Organisations. Select the option(s) that identifies (identify) the designers of the logos.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The logos are Hindustan Petroleum, Punjab National Bank and two marks built on Devanagari letterforms. They are the work of Sudarshan Dheer, Benoy Sarkar and the calligrapher R K Joshi, so the options that name only these designers, B and D, are correct. A (Ray and Keshavan) and C (Yeshwant Chaudhary, Vikas Satwalekar) name designers of other marks.

questions.text: Below are two patterns created by a repetition of circles. For each of the patterns, identify the configuration of circles from which it has been created, from the set of options given below and then answer the question that follows. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: I can be created from 3 and 4; and II can be created from 5 and 6

options.label: B
options.text: I can be created from 1 and 2; and II can be created from 5, 6 and 7

options.label: C
options.text: I can be created from 4; and II can be created from 6

options.label: D
options.text: I can be created from 4 and 5; and II can be created from 6 and 7

questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In pattern I the circle centres lie on a square grid turned through 45 degrees, nearest centres one radius times root 2 apart, so around every gap point four circles meet with centres one radius away up, down, left and right: that is configuration 4, and there is no circle centred on those points, so 5 does not fit. In pattern II the centres lie on a triangular grid one radius apart, and around the empty points six circles meet with centres one radius away at 60 degree steps: configuration 6. No circle is centred on those points, so 7 does not fit, and no square arrangement like 5 occurs. Hence I comes from 4 and II from 6.

questions.text: Shown below are schematic diagrams of a single arm of a 3-fold umbrella. Identify the correct representation/s.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: In a folding umbrella each rib section must be a pair of parallel links joined at the knuckles, so that sliding the runner folds every section in turn. In A the first section is a single bar, so the parallel pair of the second section has nothing to fold it, and in D the second section is a single bar, so the third section cannot be driven. B carries a parallel pair through every section, with one link from the top notch and one from the runner meeting the first pair. C also has pairs throughout, but its lower first bar runs straight from the runner while the upper is reached through a separate bent link, which leaves the first section free to move.

questions.text: If the following terms were to be written in the sequence: Subphylum, Class, Order, Family and Genus, which one would be correct?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: For a lion or tiger the subphylum is Vertebrata, the class is Mammalia, the order is Carnivora, the family is Felidae and the genus is Panthera. Only option D lists them in that order. Options A and C put Mammalia before Vertebrata, and B swaps the order and family.

questions.text: If [colour swatch 1] becomes [colour swatch 2], then [colour swatch 3] would become?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The teal swatch keeps its hue and saturation and only becomes darker, by roughly the same fraction in each of red, green and blue (about 82 percent of the original). Darkening the pink swatch by the same fraction gives a medium pink of the same hue. Option B matches it; A and D are darker and greyer, and C is lighter than the required shade.

questions.text: Choose the colour that should replace the question mark.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The strip blends gradually from yellow through orange towards magenta: yellow, orange, ?, salmon pink, pink, magenta. The missing step must lie halfway between the orange and the salmon pink, a muted peach orange. Option D is that in between tone; A is too pale, B is already pink, and C is too dark and saturated.

questions.text: Pick an option from the right which will correctly complete the colour pattern on the left.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The gap is a diagonal line of four hexagons running from row 3 down to row 6. The colour pattern repeats every two rows shifted three hexagons to the right, so each missing hexagon has the same colour as the hexagon two rows above it and three places to the left. That gives, from top to bottom, red, green, green, pink, which read from the bottom is pink, green, green, red: option C.

questions.text: Choose the option that would replace the question mark to correctly complete the pattern.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Each disc carries one round dot (maroon or dark olive) and one hexagon (light coral or dark red). Row 2 has the colour pairs olive with dark red, maroon with light coral, olive with light coral. Row 3 so far has olive with dark red and olive with light coral, so it repeats row 2 and the middle disc needs a maroon dot with a light coral hexagon. Column-wise the same holds, since columns 1 and 3 repeat their middle entry in the bottom row. That is option B.

questions.text: Choose the figure that should replace the question mark.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In each row the third figure keeps only the lines that appear in exactly one of the first two figures; lines common to both cancel. Row 1: top, bottom, teal diagonal and red diagonal combined with left, bottom and teal diagonal leaves left, top and red diagonal. In row 3 the first figure has top, bottom, right and teal diagonal and the second has left, teal diagonal and red diagonal. The teal diagonal cancels, leaving top, bottom, left, right and the red diagonal, which is option D.

questions.text: Choose the set of colours which is present in this painting.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The painting (in the Jamini Roy style) uses a crimson red, a dark green sari, bright yellow, a pale orange skin tone and a sky blue sari. Set D has exactly these five. A has a pure red and a bright green that do not appear, B has a tan and an electric blue, and C has a light green and an indigo that are not in the painting.

questions.text: Look carefully at the sentence given below. It is written in a specific font. From the options, choose the letter which belongs to the same font family.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Compare the details of the sentence's letters with each option: the weight of the strokes, how the ends of strokes are cut, the shape of loops and knots and how the headline joins the letters. Letter A shares these features with the sentence, so A belongs to the same font family; B, C and D differ in their loops and stroke ends.

questions.text: Which of the options would replace the missing block?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Read the grid row by row, left to right, as one long string: it repeats the nine letter block व ठ क व द व क ठ द without a break, carrying over from the end of one row to the start of the next. Row 8 starts at position 78, so its third and fourth cells are the 8th and 9th letters of the block, ठ and द. Row 9 starts at position 89, so its third and fourth cells are the 1st and 2nd letters, व and ठ. The missing block is ठ द over व ठ, option A.

questions.text: Find the odd one out among the letters below.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: All four are serif capital A letters of the same height. A, B and D are the same typeface. In C the thin left stroke is noticeably thinner, the crossbar sits a little lower and the base serifs are narrower, so it comes from a different typeface and is the odd one out.

questions.text: Given below is are three matrices with dots, the dots are arranged using a particular logic. Identify the logic and choose the option that matches the logic of the matrices.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In every row of the three given matrices there is exactly one hollow dot, and it never touches another dot in its row: the cells immediately to its left and right are always empty. In A the first row has a hollow dot right next to a filled one, in B the first row has a hollow dot between two filled ones, and in D the third row has a hollow dot touching a filled one. Only C follows the rule in all five rows.

questions.text: Choose the option that follows the logic of the hatch sequence shown below.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Each 3 by 3 grid has three rows of hatched squares. From one figure to the next, the rows move up by one (the top row goes to the bottom) and every hatch turns through 90 degrees, so horizontal becomes vertical and one diagonal becomes the other. Applying this to the third figure (rows: right-leaning diagonals, left-leaning diagonals, horizontal-vertical-horizontal) gives rows of right-leaning diagonals starting with a forward slash, then vertical-horizontal-vertical, then diagonals starting with a back slash. That is option B.

questions.text: Identify the stamp used for printing the sample (in blue) from the options given below.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A stamp prints the mirror image of its face, and the blue print reads as a reversed BE, so the stamp face must read BE the right way round: B or D. Turning the print upright and flipping it, the middle arm of the E sits slightly above the centre of the letter. In option B the E's middle arm is also above centre, while in D it sits below centre, so the stamp is B.

questions.text: Choose the pattern that completes the sequence shown below.
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The symmetric symbols (+, minus, =, x) never change. Of the five symbols that can be mirrored, the slash, the # and the % flip at every step (normal, mirrored, normal), while the square bracket and the round bracket flip every second step (normal, mirrored, mirrored). So in the fourth figure the slash, # and % are mirrored and both brackets are back to normal: back slash, [, mirrored #, ), mirrored %. That is option B.

questions.text: In pigment colors, if Green is Blue, Yellow is Green, Blue is White and Red is Yellow, what is the complementary color of White and Green?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: In the code, the colour called White is really Blue (Blue is White) and the colour called Green is really Yellow (Yellow is Green). Mixing blue and yellow pigments gives green. The complementary colour of green on the pigment colour wheel is red, so the answer is Red. Orange is the complement of blue and purple the complement of yellow, each of only one of the two colours.

questions.text: A square piece of paper is folded down into a triangle (as shown), after which a cut is made at a corner (again, as shown). Choose the option that shows the correct cut when the paper is unfolded.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Follow the folds: the square is folded on its diagonal, then the right-angle corner and the two sharp corners are each folded in so that their tips meet at the centre of the original square, and the small triangle that results has its right angle exactly at that centre. So the cut at the right-angle corner goes through the centre of the square and through all four original corners. Unfolding gives a small square hole at the centre, with its sides parallel to the paper's edges, and a small square notch at each of the four corners. That is option A.

questions.text:
The shapes below correspond to different numbers. Choose the option that replaces the question mark.

♥ × ♠ = ♦♣

♦♣ × ♥ = ♥♠ + ?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Treat each suit as a digit and two suits side by side as a two-digit number. More than one set of digits fits both lines: heart 3, spade 4, diamond 1, club 2 gives 12 x 3 = 34 + 2, so a club (B); heart 2, spade 7, diamond 1, club 4 gives 14 x 2 = 27 + 1, so a diamond (A). With two valid answers the question cannot be settled, and IIT Bombay dropped it, giving every candidate full marks.

questions.text: Choose the option that follows the logic of the sequence shown below.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Compare each figure with the one before it: the arms keep the same order around the centre (arrow, circle, square, pentagon, square), so each figure is the same shape turned. Find how far it turns from step to step and continue that turn. IIT Bombay's final key gives D.
questions.defect: The five figures show only two different drawings, in the order X, Y, X, X, Y, which by itself points to X again (option C). IIT Bombay's final key gives D, a third orientation of the figure, and the rule that leads to it cannot be worked out from the printed figures.

questions.text: Shown are symbols used for different functions. Identify the correct description sequence from the given choices.

options.label: B
options.text: Chemical Bonds, Computing, Aliens, War Zone

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The first symbol (three linked circles on green) is the chemical weapon symbol, the second (three blades on yellow) is the radiation trefoil for radioactive material, the third is the biohazard symbol, and the skull and crossbones marks a toxic substance. Only D names all four. The trefoil has nothing to do with computing, and the biohazard sign does not mean cosmology or aliens.

questions.text: Shown below are images that have different visual features. Identify the correct sequence of visual features associated with these images from the given choices.

options.label: A
options.text: Translational Symmetry, Asymmetric Repetition, Fractal Image, Fibonacci Series

options.label: B
options.text: Tessellation, Translational Repetition, Symmetric Repetition, Fractal Image

options.label: C
options.text: Fibonacci Series, Tiled Fractals, Figure and Ground Image, Spiral Symmetry

options.label: D
options.text: Radial Symmetry, Tessellation, Fractal Image, Rotational Repetition

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: The first image is a flower like star whose petals repeat about the centre: radial symmetry. The second is a grid of identical interlocking wavy tiles with no gaps: a tessellation. The third is the Sierpinski triangle, made of smaller copies of itself: a fractal. The fourth repeats one curled shape by turning it around a centre: rotational repetition. Only D gives this sequence; A, B and C misname the first or third image.

questions.text:
Given below are steps in a typical design process, but they seem to be mixed up. What is the most logical sequence of these steps?

I. Build a business out of the idea that is designed.
II. Building prototypes to test ideas and get feedback.
III. Analysis of the findings, looking for insights and find opportunities for design.
IV. Finding a need and locating a problem to solve and trying to understanding the problem by conducting research.
V. Product and technology development.
VI. Ideation and coming out with initial concepts.

options.label: A
options.text: I, IV, VI, V, III, II

options.label: B
options.text: IV, VI, III, II, V, I

options.label: C
options.text: IV, III, VI, II, V, I

options.label: D
options.text: VI, IV, III, II, I, V

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: A design process starts by finding a need and researching the problem (IV), then analysing the findings for insights and opportunities (III). Only then come ideas and initial concepts (VI), which are tested through prototypes (II). The chosen idea goes into product and technology development (V) and finally becomes a business (I). That is IV, III, VI, II, V, I, option C. B puts ideation before analysis, and A and D start in the wrong place.

questions.text:
Given below is a write-up on the discovery of the Mouse. But the sentences seem to be mixed up. What is the correct logical sequence of these sentences?

I. We use the mouse not just because Doug Engelbart invented it, but because it turned out to be the pointing device that performed best for pointing and clicking on a display, outperforming light pens, cursor keys, joysticks, trackballs, and everything else that was tried in early tests with users.
II. Years later, when he was searching for a device to select objects on a computer screen, he remembered those notes, and together with Bill English, he built the first mouse.
III. He was bored at a conference, and wrote in his notebook about putting two wheels at right angles to track movement on a plane.
IV. The mouse won because it was the easiest to use.
V. When he was a student, he was measuring the area under some complex-shaped curves, using a device with wheels that would roll in one direction and slide sideways in the axis at ninety degrees.
VI. Doug Engelbart tells the story of how he invented the mouse.

options.label: A
options.text: I, IV, VI, V, III, II

options.label: B
options.text: VI, V, III, II, I, IV

options.label: C
options.text: VI, I, IV, III, V, II

options.label: D
options.text: IV, I, VI, V, III, II

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: VI introduces the story, so it comes first. The story runs in time order: as a student he used a wheeled measuring device (V), later at a conference he noted the idea of two wheels at right angles (III), and years later he remembered those notes and built the mouse (II). The write-up then explains why the mouse is still used (I), and IV sums it up: it won because it was the easiest to use. That is VI, V, III, II, I, IV, option B. D cannot be right because IV only makes sense after I has listed the devices it beat.

questions.text:
Read the following statements related to the earth's environment

I. Water vapour, and not carbon dioxide, is the most prevalent greenhouse gas in the earth's atmosphere.
II. Besides China and the United States, India and Brazil are the highest greenhouse emitting countries.
III. Although about 70% of the Earth is covered by water, and there's more beneath the surface, only about 5% of earth's water is fresh, liquid and found above ground.
IV. Globally birth rates are fluctuating, people are living longer and the total population is increasing.

Which of the above statements are TRUE?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: I is true: water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas. IV is true in substance: people are living longer and world population keeps rising. II is false: after China and the United States the next largest emitters are the European Union, India and Russia, not Brazil. III is false: only about 2.5 to 3 percent of the earth's water is fresh, and fresh liquid water above ground is well under 1 percent. So I and IV, option D.

questions.text:
Read the following statements related to the economy

I. Rebuilding efforts in the wake of natural disasters can give a boost to the economy.
II. An increase in consumer spending is most likely to cause a decrease in employment.
III. Carbon trading helps reduce carbon emissions mainly because low polluters buy excess permits to pollute and high polluters are fined by the carbon regulator.
IV. Economic growth of a nation increases the demand for labour, thereby raising income levels.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Only IV is true: economic growth raises the demand for labour, which pushes incomes up. I is the broken-window fallacy: rebuilding replaces what the disaster destroyed and diverts spending from other uses, so it does not make the economy better off. II is wrong because more consumer spending raises demand and so tends to increase employment. III is wrong because in carbon trading it is the high polluters who must buy permits from low polluters, which rewards cutting emissions. So the answer is C.

questions.text:
Read the following design context:

The city of Mumbai is facing a severe shortage of parking spaces. The problem is acute in south Mumbai where land is expensive and undeveloped land almost non-existent. A panel of experts consisting of city and town planners, transportation engineers and designers, economists, historians and policy makers has studied the problem carefully and has recommended a set of measures:

I. Start a free public bicycle program in which people are encouraged to use public transport for longer distances and shared common bicycles for shorter distances.
II. Allow people to download a mobile App which will allow vehicle owners to book parking spots up to one week in advance.
III. Ban vehicles with even registration numbers on the even days of the month, and odd registration numbers on odd days of the month.
IV. Make parking prohibitively expensive.
V. Build more multi-storied and underground parking complexes.
VI. Declare the whole of south Mumbai as a heritage district to prevent any further construction and limit vehicle entry by imposing toll.
VII. Design self-parking vehicles.
VIII. Create a car pooling mobile App that will connect people to share cars and reduce the number of cars on the road.
IX. Make the roads more pedestrian-friendly.
X. Institute a parking pricing mechanism which dynamically adjusts the cost of parking based on demand and supply.

Identify FOUR recommendations that will make the most impact in solving the parking problem.
questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: Look for measures that cut the number of cars that need parking or add space without needing new land. A free public bicycle scheme linked to public transport (I) moves trips out of cars, odd-even rules (III) take about half the cars off the road on any day, multi-storied and underground parking (V) adds spaces on the same land, and dynamic pricing (X) keeps the existing spaces turning over. The other measures either do not reduce demand for parking (an advance-booking app, self-parking cars) or act only bluntly or indirectly. So the answer is D.

questions.text: Identify which option given below can be folded to make the 3D object in the picture shown below.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Count the faces of the solid first: each polygon end comes in a pair, and every edge of the outline gives one square side face. Then check each net for the right number of each shape and see whether the squares wrap round to meet the polygons edge to edge. IIT Bombay's final key gives B.
questions.defect: As drawn, the solid appears to be a pentagonal prism, a cube and a hexagonal prism joined in a row, which needs 13 square faces besides its two pentagons and two hexagons; the nets have 14, 16, 16 and 15 squares, so none folds into it exactly. IIT Bombay's final key gives B, but which solid it intends cannot be settled from the printed figure.

questions.text: Figures 1 to 5 are views of a cube. From the options given below, choose the sixth view of the cube in the series.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The mark (one long and one short line) moves left face, right face, top face, then left, right, top again, so view 6 has it on the top face. The views come in pairs: 2 is the mirror image of 1, 4 is the mirror image of 3 and the next view is the mirror image of 5, each mirror line running through the corner nearest to us. Reflecting view 5 (lines from the outer right edge, long line at the top) across the line through the right-hand corner puts the lines on the back-right edge of the top face, with the long line nearer the right corner. That is option B.

questions.text: Figure 1 shows an unfolded cuboid. Below it are four options showing four fully-folded cuboids. Identify the cuboid that can be unfolded as Figure 1.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In the net the top face is attached to the fourth side face (a diagonal band), so its stripes run parallel to the edges it shares with the two diagonal faces. In every option the top's stripes run parallel to the edge shared with the right-hand face, so the right-hand face must be a diagonal face. Only B shows a diagonal on the right face. Its left face has the thin stripe away from the corner and the thick one near it, which is the first side face of the net, and the thick stripe on top sits away from that diagonal face, as in the net. So B is correct.

questions.text: The image below shows a 3D object. Only one of the options shows the same object from a different view. Identify it.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Build the object in your mind from its cubes: two parallel bars with arms of different lengths attached at different heights. Turn it and compare each option arm by arm, checking the length of each arm and which bar it leaves from. Option A shows the same object from another side. B is missing one cube from an arm, and C and D attach an arm at the wrong place.

questions.text:
Read the three statements below and the conclusions deduced from these statements.

Statements:
All Surrealists are melted clocks.
Some melted clocks are Dalis.
All Dalis are macabre works.

Conclusions:
(i) Some macabre works are Dalis.
(ii) Some macabre works are melted clocks.
(iii) Some Dalis are Surrealist.

Based on the above, which of the conclusions definitely follows from the statements?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Some melted clocks are Dalis, so Dalis exist, and every Dali is a macabre work: so some macabre works are Dalis, and (i) follows. The melted clocks that are Dalis are also macabre works, so some macabre works are melted clocks, and (ii) follows. Nothing links Dalis to Surrealists: the Dalis could be melted clocks that are not Surrealists, so (iii) does not follow. Only (i) and (ii) follow.

questions.text:
Select the option that best explains how the two statements below are related.

The fiction novel, Gone Girl, by Gillian Flynn, was very popular.

It was on several bestseller lists in the US for over 34 weeks in 2012, and later made into a movie.

options.label: A
options.text: The first sentence contradicts the second.

options.label: B
options.text: The first sentence explains the meaning of the second.

options.label: C
options.text: The second sentence explains why the book is popular.

options.label: D
options.text: The second sentence provides evidence for the first.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The first sentence makes a claim: the novel was very popular. The second gives facts that show this: months on bestseller lists and a film adaptation. It does not say why readers liked the book, so it is evidence for the claim rather than a reason. Nothing contradicts, and the first sentence does not explain the second.

questions.text: The building shown in Picture 1 can look as it does in Picture 2 if photographed using:
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: In Picture 1 the vertical columns lean inwards because the camera was tilted up at the building. In Picture 2 they are parallel. A tilt-shift lens lets the lens shift upwards while the camera back stays vertical, which removes this converging-verticals effect. A mirror lens is a compact telephoto, USM is an autofocus motor, and a stereoscopic lens makes 3D image pairs; none corrects perspective.

questions.text: Three views of a block with seven different shapes printed on its surfaces are shown below. Find the same block from the options given.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The block is a house shape with 7 faces: 2 roof faces, 2 walls, 2 gable ends and a base. View 2 shows a gable (rectangle) with the bow-tie roof on its left and the hexagon roof on its right, and View 1 confirms the bow-tie roof sits above the circle wall next to the rectangle gable. View 3 shows the other gable (star) with the circle wall and the bar on the base, so the face never seen (the triangle) is the wall under the hexagon roof. Looking at the star gable from outside, the wall on its left is the triangle wall with the hexagon roof above it, which is option A. B puts the star on a wall, C puts the triangle on a gable, and D swaps the circle and the square.

questions.text: The green arrow is pointing at a mark on a DSLR camera body. What does this mark represent?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The circle crossed by a line on the top of a camera body is the focal plane mark. It shows where the sensor (or film) sits inside the body, so close-up focusing distances can be measured from it. It is not a focus, aperture or firmware setting.

questions.text: The image below shows a product designed by Raymond Loewy. Identify the product.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: This is Raymond Loewy's streamlined pencil sharpener of 1933, a famous example of streamlining applied to an everyday object. The wooden handle on the side is the crank and the hole at the front takes the pencil. It is not an engine, a toy or a decal.

questions.text: These are modified images by famous artists. Identify the correct sequence of artists of the original images.

options.label: A
options.text: Leonardo da Vinci, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Michaelangelo

options.label: B
options.text: Michaelangelo, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Leonardo da Vinci

options.label: C
options.text: Michaelangelo, Rembrandt, Van Gogh, Leonardo da Vinci

options.label: D
options.text: Leonardo da Vinci, Rembrandt, Van Gogh, Michaelangelo

questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Image A parodies The Creation of Adam by Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel). Image B parodies Girl with a Pearl Earring by Vermeer. Image C copies the swirling brushwork of a Van Gogh self-portrait. Image D is Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man. So the order is Michelangelo, Vermeer, Van Gogh, Leonardo da Vinci.

questions.text: These images are made using different art techniques. Identify the correct sequence of techniques from options below.
questions.subject: Environment and Society
questions.solution: Image A has soft, transparent washes with blooms where colours run into each other, which is watercolour. Image B has waxy strokes with paper showing through, typical of crayon. Image C has flat, bright layers, typical of acrylic, and image D has thick, blended strokes with rich depth, typical of oil paint. Only option C starts with watercolour, and its sequence fits all four.

questions.text:
Given below are steps to tie a shoelace, but the steps seem to be mixed up. What is the correct logical sequence of these steps?

1. Pass one end of the shoelace under the other.
2. Pull tight.
3. Hold one end of each shoelace in each hand.
4. Cross them, making an X.
5. Bend it into a flat loop and pull through, making a bow.
6. Fold one shoelace in half while holding laces taut.
7. Grasp it in the middle after pulling it around the folded end.
8. Wrap the other end around the folded end.

The Correct Order is:
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: First hold one end in each hand (3), cross them into an X (4), pass one end under the other (1) and pull tight (2) to make the first knot. Then fold one lace into a loop (6), wrap the other end around it (8), grasp it in the middle (7) and push it through as a second loop to form the bow (5). That is 3, 4, 1, 2, 6, 8, 7, 5.

questions.text:
Given below is a list of sixteen idioms which originated from sports. Each option contains four sports. Identify the option that has all its four sports represented in at least one of the idioms in the list.

i. Back to square one
ii. Ball in his court
iii. Below par
iv. Breaking one’s duck
v. Down to the wire
vi. Full court press
vii. Going the distance
viii. Jump the gun
ix. Level playing field
x. On the back foot
xi. Play it close to one's chest
xii. Pole position
xiii. Saved by the bell

xv. Throw in the towel
xvi. Touché

options.label: B

options.label: D
